demoniac-in-synagogue-mrk.quote: Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be quiet, and come out of him!”
details: This is the first thing Jesus does in Mark's Gospel after calling His first disciples.
It happens in a synagogue, during a service.
The unclean spirit knew exactly who He was before anyone else did.
demoniac-in-synagogue-mrk.whatHappened: In the synagogue at Capernaum, a man with an unclean spirit cried out — naming Jesus correctly, which nobody else in the room had done. Jesus told it to be quiet and come out. It convulsed the man and left, and the congregation were left asking each other what they had just seen.
demoniac-in-synagogue-mrk.hopeMeaning: The first person in Mark to say plainly who Jesus is happens to be the thing being driven out. Right belief and right standing are not the same thing here — which is oddly freeing for anyone who has assumed that understanding God correctly is the whole of it.
demoniac-in-synagogue-mrk.reflectionQuestion: Is there something you believe to be true about God that has not yet changed how you live?
demoniac-in-synagogue-mrk.distinctive: Mark opens his account of Jesus' work with this — it is the first miracle in his Gospel, placed before any healing, and the crowd's reaction is about authority rather than compassion. Luke tells the same scene but Mark alone makes it the opening move, so the whole Gospel begins with something being confronted rather than someone being comforted.

peters-mother-in-law-mrk.quote: He came and took her by the hand and raised her up. The fever left her immediately, and she served them.
details: They told Him about her at once, as soon as they came into the house.
He took her by the hand and raised her up rather than speaking.
That evening the whole town gathered at the door.
peters-mother-in-law-mrk.whatHappened: Coming out of the synagogue into Peter's house, they told Jesus at once that Peter's wife's mother was in bed with a fever. He took her by the hand and raised her up; the fever left, and she got up and served them.
peters-mother-in-law-mrk.hopeMeaning: Someone mentioned it immediately, without waiting to see whether it was worth mentioning. The whole exchange is a few seconds long and needs no build-up.
peters-mother-in-law-mrk.reflectionQuestion: What would you mention straight away, if you assumed it was worth mentioning?
peters-mother-in-law-mrk.distinctive: Mark uses the language of raising — took her by the hand and raised her up — the same verb he will use for the dead. Matthew has only a touch; Luke has Jesus stand over her and rebuke the fever as though addressing a spirit. Mark also alone sets it immediately after the synagogue confrontation, so the public act and the domestic one sit side by side in one afternoon.

leper-cleansed-mrk.quote: Being moved with compassion, He stretched out His hand, and touched him, and said to him, “I want to. Be made clean.”
details: Mark says outright what moved Him: compassion.
Jesus warned him sternly to say nothing.
He told everyone, and as a result Jesus could no longer enter a town openly.
leper-cleansed-mrk.whatHappened: A man with leprosy knelt and said Jesus could make him clean if He were willing. Moved with compassion, Jesus touched him and said He was willing. Then He warned him sternly to tell nobody — and the man told everyone, until Jesus could no longer go into a town openly and stayed out in deserted places.
leper-cleansed-mrk.hopeMeaning: The healed man's joy cost Jesus his freedom of movement, and the account records that without rebuking him for it. Some consequences of good news are inconvenient and are borne anyway.
leper-cleansed-mrk.reflectionQuestion: Has your gratitude ever cost someone else something?
leper-cleansed-mrk.distinctive: Mark alone names the emotion — moved with compassion — and alone follows the story past the healing to its cost: the man's talking meant Jesus could no longer enter a city openly. Matthew ends at the instruction to show himself to the priest; Luke adds that Jesus withdrew to pray. Mark is the one who tells you what it did to Jesus' movements afterwards.

paralytic-mrk.quote: When they could not come near to Him for the crowd, they removed the roof where He was. When they had broken it up, they let down the mat that the paralytic was lying on.
details: Four men carried him, and the house was too crowded to get in.
They dug through someone's roof rather than wait.
Jesus responded to their faith — the carriers' — not the paralysed man's.
paralytic-mrk.whatHappened: Four men carried a paralysed friend to the house where Jesus was teaching and could not get through the crowd. So they went up, broke open the roof, and lowered him through it. Jesus saw their faith and spoke first about forgiveness, then told the man to get up and walk home.
paralytic-mrk.hopeMeaning: The faith the text credits belongs to the men on the roof. Someone else's determination is what put him in front of Jesus, and that counted.
paralytic-mrk.reflectionQuestion: Whose determination has put you somewhere you could not have got to alone?
paralytic-mrk.distinctive: Mark gives the four carriers and the broken roof in full detail — the crowd, the digging, the mat lowered through the hole. Matthew leaves the roof out entirely and simply says they brought him; Luke has them go up and remove tiles. Mark is the one who makes you feel the effort and the damage done to somebody's house.

withered-hand-mrk.quote: When he had looked around at them with anger, being grieved at the hardening of their hearts, he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.”
details: He asked whether it was lawful to do good or harm on the Sabbath, and nobody answered.
Mark records Jesus angry — and grieved — in the same sentence.
The response to the healing was a plot to destroy Him.
withered-hand-mrk.whatHappened: In the synagogue, watched by people looking for a charge, Jesus asked whether the Sabbath was for doing good or harm, for saving life or killing. Nobody answered. He looked round at them, angry and grieved, and told the man to stretch out his hand. It was restored — and the watchers went straight out to plan His death.
withered-hand-mrk.hopeMeaning: Mark lets Jesus be angry, and says the anger was grief at hard hearts rather than at the men themselves. Anger and grief turn out to be the same thing here, aimed at what people had become rather than at who they were.
withered-hand-mrk.reflectionQuestion: Is there anger in you that is really grief about something?
withered-hand-mrk.distinctive: Mark alone records the anger and the grief on Jesus' face, and alone ends with the Pharisees conspiring with the Herodians to destroy Him — an alliance of enemies. Matthew argues the case first with the sheep in a pit; Luke notes it was the right hand. Mark makes the scene about hardness meeting silence.

gerasene-demoniac-mrk.quote: He asked him, “What is your name?” He said to him, “My name is Legion, for we are many.”
details: He had broken every chain and fetter used on him; nobody had the strength to restrain him.
He lived among the tombs, crying out night and day and cutting himself with stones.
Afterwards he was found sitting, clothed, and in his right mind.
gerasene-demoniac-mrk.whatHappened: A man lived among the tombs, uncontainable, howling day and night and cutting himself. He ran and knelt before Jesus. Asked its name, what held him answered Legion. It was sent into a herd of pigs, which drowned. When the townspeople came, the man was sitting there dressed and in his right mind — and they asked Jesus to leave.
gerasene-demoniac-mrk.hopeMeaning: Mark spends more words on how bad it had been than on the deliverance itself, which is why the picture of him sitting and clothed lands so hard. The account also refuses a neat ending: he asks to come along and is told to go home and tell his own people instead.
gerasene-demoniac-mrk.reflectionQuestion: Would you rather be sent somewhere new, or sent back to the people who knew you before?
gerasene-demoniac-mrk.distinctive: Mark gives the fullest and grimmest history: the chains torn apart, the nights in the mountains, the self-harm, and the name Legion. Matthew has two men and no backstory at all; Luke keeps the name but compresses the suffering. Mark alone ends with the man begging to go with Jesus and being told to stay and tell his own household.

jairus-daughter-mrk.quote: Taking the child by the hand, he said to her, “Talitha cumi!” Which means, being interpreted, “Girl, I tell you, get up!”
details: The father is named — Jairus — and is a synagogue official.
Word came mid-journey that the girl had died, and that there was no point troubling the teacher.
Mark keeps the actual Aramaic words spoken, and notes she was twelve years old.
jairus-daughter-mrk.whatHappened: Jairus, a synagogue ruler, begged Jesus to come for his dying daughter. On the way, messengers said she had died and there was no point continuing. Jesus told him not to be afraid, only believe. At the house He put out the mourners, took the girl's hand, and said in Aramaic: little girl, get up. She did — and He told them to give her something to eat.
jairus-daughter-mrk.hopeMeaning: The message on the road is the hardest sentence in the story: don't bother the teacher any more. Jairus is told to keep believing precisely after the reason for hope has gone. And at the end, the miracle finishes with someone remembering the child would be hungry.
jairus-daughter-mrk.reflectionQuestion: What would it take to keep walking after the news that it is too late?
jairus-daughter-mrk.distinctive: Mark alone preserves the Aramaic — Talitha cumi — as though remembering the exact sound of it, and alone adds that Jesus told them to give her something to eat. He names Jairus, where Matthew leaves him an unnamed ruler, and he alone gives the interval on the road where the news arrives and the father has to decide whether to keep going.

feeding-5000-mrk.quote: They took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and also of the fish.
details: Jesus had tried to take the disciples somewhere quiet to rest; the crowd got there first.
Mark says He was moved because they were like sheep without a shepherd.
They sat down in groups on green grass.
feeding-5000-mrk.whatHappened: Jesus had taken the disciples away to rest, and the crowd arrived ahead of them. Seeing them like sheep without a shepherd, He taught them, and then fed five thousand from five loaves and two fish. They sat in groups on the green grass, and twelve baskets of scraps were gathered.
feeding-5000-mrk.hopeMeaning: The attempt to rest failed, and He taught and fed them anyway. Mark's reason is not that they were hungry but that they had no one leading them — the meal answers a loneliness as much as an appetite.
feeding-5000-mrk.reflectionQuestion: Is what you are hungry for actually food, or something more like being led?
feeding-5000-mrk.distinctive: Mark alone explains the motive — they were like sheep without a shepherd — and alone notices the green grass and the people sitting in orderly groups of hundreds and fifties. John names the boy and the barley; Matthew counts the women and children. Mark gives you the picture of the hillside itself.

walking-on-water-mrk.quote: He got into the boat with them; and the wind ceased, and they were very amazed among themselves, and marveled.
details: He saw them straining at the oars against a headwind, from the shore, at night.
Mark says He intended to pass by them.
The account ends by saying they had not understood about the loaves.
walking-on-water-mrk.whatHappened: Late in the night, seeing the disciples struggling against the wind, Jesus came to them walking on the sea — and would have passed by. They saw Him, thought He was a ghost, and cried out. He spoke to them, got into the boat, and the wind dropped. Mark ends by noting they still had not understood about the loaves.
walking-on-water-mrk.hopeMeaning: He saw them straining before they saw Him. And Mark ends not on triumph but on hearts that had not caught up — the wonder happened and they still did not understand. That is recorded without embarrassment.
walking-on-water-mrk.reflectionQuestion: Is there something you have seen God do that you still have not really absorbed?
walking-on-water-mrk.distinctive: Mark alone says He meant to pass by them, and alone ends on the flat verdict that their hearts were hardened because they had not understood about the loaves. Matthew turns the same night into Peter's walk and rescue; John shortens it to the boat reaching shore. Mark's version is the one where nothing is resolved inside the men.

canaanite-daughter-mrk.quote: He said to her, “For this saying, go your way. The demon has gone out of your daughter.”
details: Mark identifies her as a Greek, a Syrophoenician by race.
Jesus had gone into that region wanting nobody to know He was there.
She went home and found the child on the bed, well.
canaanite-daughter-mrk.whatHappened: In foreign territory, where He had gone hoping to stay unnoticed, a Greek woman found Jesus and begged for her daughter. What He said sounded like a refusal about children's bread and dogs. She answered that even the dogs under the table get the crumbs. He told her that for that saying she could go home — and she found the child well.
canaanite-daughter-mrk.hopeMeaning: He tells her it is her saying that settles it. She argued, and the argument was received rather than corrected. There is room here for people who talk back.
canaanite-daughter-mrk.reflectionQuestion: Do you think of arguing with God as faithlessness, or as a kind of faith?
canaanite-daughter-mrk.distinctive: Mark names her by nationality — a Greek, a Syrophoenician — and sets the scene with Jesus trying to go unnoticed in foreign territory. He also ends inside her house, with the mother arriving home to find the child laid on the bed and well. Matthew calls her a Canaanite, adds the disciples urging Him to send her away, and stays outside with the crowd.

deaf-and-mute-mrk.quote: Looking up to heaven, he sighed, and said to him, “Ephphatha!” That is, “Be opened!”
details: Jesus took him away from the crowd, privately, before doing anything.
He used touch — fingers in the ears, spittle on the tongue — with a man who could not hear words.
Mark records that Jesus sighed.
deaf-and-mute-mrk.whatHappened: People brought a man who was deaf and could barely speak, and asked Jesus to lay a hand on him. Jesus took him away from the crowd on his own, put fingers in his ears, touched his tongue, looked up, sighed, and said: be opened. The man heard, and spoke clearly.
deaf-and-mute-mrk.hopeMeaning: Everything here is adapted to the man in front of Him. He is taken out of the crowd, and communicated with by touch rather than speech, because speech was no use to him. The method fits the person, not the occasion.
deaf-and-mute-mrk.reflectionQuestion: Where might you need to change how you communicate rather than what you are saying?
deaf-and-mute-mrk.distinctive: This healing appears only in Mark. So does the sigh, and the Aramaic word itself — Ephphatha — which he keeps and then translates, the same instinct that made him preserve Talitha cumi.

feeding-4000-mrk.quote: They ate and were filled. They took up seven baskets of broken pieces that were left over.
details: The crowd had been with Him three days already.
This is in Gentile territory, unlike the feeding of the five thousand.
Seven loaves, a few small fish, and seven baskets left over.
feeding-4000-mrk.whatHappened: A crowd of about four thousand had been with Jesus three days with nothing left to eat, and He said He would not send them away hungry. From seven loaves and a few small fish they all ate and were filled, and seven baskets of pieces were gathered.
feeding-4000-mrk.hopeMeaning: He does this twice, and the second time is on the other side of the lake, among people not His own. The repetition is the point: it was not a one-off performance for a home crowd.
feeding-4000-mrk.reflectionQuestion: Do you find it harder to believe God would do something for you twice?
feeding-4000-mrk.distinctive: Mark and Matthew both keep this second feeding. Mark places it firmly in Gentile territory and follows it with Jesus asking the disciples, twice over, whether they remember how many baskets were left each time. In Mark the story is aimed at the disciples' memory as much as at the crowd's hunger.

blind-at-bethsaida-mrk.quote: He looked up, and said, “I see men, but I see them like walking trees.”
details: Jesus led him by the hand out of the village before doing anything.
After the first touch his sight was real but not yet clear.
It took a second touch before he saw everyone clearly.
blind-at-bethsaida-mrk.whatHappened: At Bethsaida a blind man was brought to Jesus. He took him by the hand, led him out of the village, and touched his eyes. Asked what he saw, the man said people looked like walking trees. Jesus laid hands on him again, and he saw everything clearly.
blind-at-bethsaida-mrk.hopeMeaning: This is the only healing in the Gospels that happens in two stages, and the man is honest at the halfway point rather than pretending it was finished. Partial progress is allowed to be named as partial.
blind-at-bethsaida-mrk.reflectionQuestion: Where are you partway through something, and tempted to claim it is complete?
blind-at-bethsaida-mrk.distinctive: Only Mark records this, and only Mark records a healing that needed a second attempt. He is also the one who has Jesus take the man by the hand and lead him out of the village first — the same private, unhurried handling as the deaf man a chapter earlier.

transfiguration-mrk.quote: His clothing became glistening, exceedingly white, like snow, such as no launderer on earth can whiten them.
details: Mark reaches for a laundry comparison to describe it.
Peter spoke because he did not know what to say, not because he had something to say.
Then suddenly there was nobody there but Jesus.
transfiguration-mrk.whatHappened: On a high mountain, alone with three of His disciples, Jesus was changed in front of them, His clothes impossibly white. Elijah and Moses appeared and talked with Him. Peter offered to build three shelters — Mark explains he simply did not know what to say. A cloud came, a voice spoke, and then there was nobody there but Jesus.
transfiguration-mrk.hopeMeaning: Mark describes glory by reaching for a laundry, which is either a failure of language or the most honest thing available. And he excuses Peter's babbling by saying plainly that the man was terrified and out of his depth.
transfiguration-mrk.reflectionQuestion: When have you filled a silence because you could not bear not knowing what to say?
transfiguration-mrk.distinctive: Mark's comparison is domestic and slightly awkward — whiter than any launderer on earth could get them. He also alone explains Peter's suggestion as panic: he did not know what to say, for they were very afraid. Matthew has the disciples fall on their faces and Jesus touch them; Luke notes they were heavy with sleep. Mark leaves them simply frightened and talking nonsense.

boy-with-demon-mrk.quote: Immediately the father of the child cried out with tears, “I believe. Help my unbelief!”
details: Jesus asked the father how long it had been happening: since childhood.
The father's request begins "if you can do anything" — and Jesus repeats the phrase back.
After it left, the boy looked dead, and Jesus took him by the hand and raised him.
boy-with-demon-mrk.whatHappened: A father brought a son the disciples could not help. Asked how long it had gone on, he said since childhood — and asked Jesus to help if He could do anything. Jesus took up the word "if", and the father cried out that he believed and needed help with his unbelief. The boy was freed, looked dead, and was raised up by the hand.
boy-with-demon-mrk.hopeMeaning: The most quoted sentence here is a contradiction said out loud through tears, and it is treated as sufficient. Belief and unbelief in the same breath did not disqualify him.
boy-with-demon-mrk.reflectionQuestion: Could you say both halves of that sentence honestly today?
boy-with-demon-mrk.distinctive: This is Mark's set piece. He alone gives the father's history — since childhood, into fire and water — and alone records the exchange over the word "if", and the tearful "I believe; help my unbelief." Matthew answers the disciples' failure with the mustard seed instead; Luke shortens the whole encounter. The father is at the centre only in Mark.

blind-at-jericho-mrk.quote: He, casting away his cloak, sprang up, and came to Jesus.
details: The man is named: Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus, a beggar by the road.
The crowd told him to be quiet and he shouted louder.
A beggar's cloak was his livelihood — he threw it aside to get up.
blind-at-jericho-mrk.whatHappened: Blind Bartimaeus was begging by the road out of Jericho and began shouting for mercy. The crowd told him to be quiet; he shouted more. Jesus stopped and called him. He threw off his cloak, jumped up, and came. Asked what he wanted, he said he wanted to see — and afterwards followed Jesus down the road.
blind-at-jericho-mrk.hopeMeaning: The cloak was the tool of his trade, spread out to catch coins, and he threw it away before he could see well enough to find it again. Something in the calling made holding onto it unnecessary.
blind-at-jericho-mrk.reflectionQuestion: What would you have to put down in order to get up quickly?
blind-at-jericho-mrk.distinctive: Mark names him — Bartimaeus — where Matthew has two anonymous men and Luke one. Mark alone has the cloak thrown aside and the man springing up, and alone reports what the crowd said when they called him over: cheer up, get up, he is calling you. The scene is full of movement in Mark and static in the others.

fig-tree-mrk.quote: Seeing a fig tree afar off having leaves, he came to see if perhaps he might find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs.
details: Mark says plainly that it was not the season for figs.
The tree was cursed on the way into Jerusalem, before the temple was cleared.
Only the next morning did they pass it again and find it withered from the roots.
fig-tree-mrk.whatHappened: Hungry on the road into Jerusalem, Jesus saw a fig tree in leaf, went to it and found nothing — and Mark adds that it was not the season for figs anyway. He said no one would eat from it again. That day He cleared the temple. The next morning they passed the tree and found it withered from the roots, and Peter pointed it out.
fig-tree-mrk.hopeMeaning: This is a hard passage and Mark makes it harder by noting it was not fig season. It is not a story about a tree failing to perform on demand. Mark wraps it around the temple to say what it is really about — something in full leaf that had no fruit on it.
fig-tree-mrk.reflectionQuestion: Is there something in your life in full leaf that you know has no fruit on it?
fig-tree-mrk.distinctive: Mark splits the story across two days and puts the clearing of the temple in the middle, so the tree becomes a frame for the temple rather than an incident on the road. He alone admits it was not the season for figs. Matthew joins the halves together and has it wither immediately, and keeps the focus on prayer and faith.

resurrection-mrk.quote: Don’t be amazed. You seek Jesus, the Nazarene, who has been crucified. He has risen! He is not here. See the place where they laid Him!
details: The women set out worrying about who would roll the stone away.
They found it already rolled back, and a young man in white sitting inside.
The message singled out Peter by name — the one who had denied Him.
resurrection-mrk.whatHappened: After the Sabbath the women came with spices, worrying on the way about who would move the stone. It was already rolled back. Inside, a young man in white told them He had risen, showed them the empty place, and sent them to tell the disciples — and Peter. They fled trembling, and said nothing to anyone, because they were afraid.
resurrection-mrk.hopeMeaning: The message names Peter specifically, days after he had denied knowing Jesus three times. Being singled out by name in the first announcement is the opposite of what he would have expected.
resurrection-mrk.reflectionQuestion: If a message came for you and one other person by name, would you assume it was good news?
resurrection-mrk.distinctive: Mark's account ends in fear and silence — they said nothing to anyone — which is a startling place to stop a Gospel. He alone has the women worrying about the stone on the way, and alone records the instruction to tell "His disciples and Peter". Matthew has an earthquake and guards; Luke two men in dazzling clothes; John has Mary weeping alone. Mark leaves it unresolved.
